newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 13.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- INFLATION STAYS ABOVE TARGET

Figures from the Office for National Statistics have revealed that inflation for the month of November remained at a steady underlying rate of 3.3 per cent, a level unchanged from October when a rise was written off by the chancellor as a one-time aberration. The fact that the figure remained the same for November has prompted speculation that Kenneth Clarke may soon be forced to raise interest rates. At the same time UK manufacturers announced that export earnings had fallen to their lowest level for nearly three years as the strength of sterling impacted on overseas demand.
-- WICKES ENDS UNCERTAINTY WITH 53 MILLION STG RIGHTS ISSUE

The beleaguered DIY chain Wickes has announced that it is to attempt to raise some 53.2 million stg in a discounted rights issue. The company will also embark on a capital reconstruction as it attempts to improve its balance sheet in the wake of accounting problems that led to it overstating profit levels for over three years. If the company's plans are approved by the High Court it would result in the resumption of trading in Wickes shares on January 7.
-- GERMANY SETS TOUGH TERMS FOR EMU DEAL

On the eve of the opening of a Dublin summit of EU leaders last minute efforts are being made to convince Germany to alter its position vis a vis the proposed post-Emu stability pact, designed to secure budgetary discipline among participating states. Chancellor Kohl is keen to see any such pact enforced rigidly, with countries running high deficits being the subject of automatic and heavy financial penalties. The rest of the EU is considerably less keen on such an approach, preferring to see a more flexible approach adopted.
-- TRADING POWERS IN MOVE TO SCRAP IT TARIFFS BY 2000

At the WTO summit in Singapore the four leading producers of information technology, the US, Japan, Canada and the EU, have all agreed on a plan that will seek to remove tariffs on international trade in IT products by the end of the decade. The four have insisted, however, that in order to work the deal will have to be endorsed by countries accounting for 90 per cent of world trade in this sector. The accord has come after the US was persuaded to add a range of products to the list covered.
-- POLLY PECK ASSET FIGHT GOES TO EUROPEAN COURT

Administrators of the failed Polly Peck group are to go to the European Court for Human Rights in an effort to secure for shareholders in the company access to some of its assets held in Turkey. The move comes after efforts by Coopers & Lybrand to secure assets in Turkey were blocked by local courts on a number of occasions. The development comes at an unfortunate time for Turkey, which has already been coming under increasing international pressure over its human rights record.
-- INDUSTRY SHELVES LOBBYING SCHEME

A decision to establish a new lobbying group to represent the interests of privatized companies has been postponed until after the next general election because of concern that such a move might cause friction with the Labour party. Labour has harbored suspicions that the group is being brought together in an effort to oppose its planned windfall tax on utilities. A number of companies declined to attend an inaugural meeting of the proposed group, arranged by senior executives from British Airways and Unipart.
-- TREASURY MAY PROP UP PFI WITH CASH FOR HOSPITAL DEALS

It is reported that the Treasury is considering the provision of state funds in order to help rescue a number of private finance initiative projects in the health service which have run into difficulties. The news comes as it was revealed that two major hospitals are cancelling PFI projects after having decided they failed to represent value for money. Funding deficits have affected a number of projects in which private sources had been envisaged as being the only source of funding.
-- SCHEME TO SAVE MILLENNIUM PLAN

Final efforts are being made by the government to devise a business plan for the Millennium Festival, to be held in Greenwich, which will address concerns expressed by Labour. The festival requires the backing of both the government and the Labour party if a number of private sponsors are to proceed with the provision of funding. Companies such as British Telecom and British Airways are reluctant to proceed unless the costs of the initiative are underwritten by the government and Labour, which might be the government at the time.
-- SIB TO STUDY ELECTRONIC SHARE-TRADING RULES

The Securities and Investments Board is to examine proposed rules for the introduction of electronic share trading in London amid concerns expressed by some that the regulations will unduly favour investment banks. Key to the objections are rules governing how soon and how much data must be provided by banks which have engaged in large block share deals. At present it is envisaged that the banks will be allowed a 60 minute delay before details of such deals appear on trading screens.
-- IBM's 350 MILLION DOLLAR FACTORY WILL BE RECORD IRISH INWARD INVESTMENT

IBM has announced that it is to invest some 350 million dollars in setting up a computer memory disc plant in the Republic of Ireland. The company was attracted to the country by a range of factors, including a low rate of corporate tax, plentiful skilled workers and access to EU markets. It is thought that the investment will result in the creation of several thousand jobs. Last year Ireland managed to secure 30 per cent of all US high technology inward investments into the EU.
